content.text:
The case-study Overview is rebuilt to match the Figma frames and works for all three projects. The changes are on a new branch on top of the stack, `fix/figma-case-study-overview`, and are uncommitted. I compared against Figma's coordinates at 1440×1171, and nearly everything lands within about a pixel. That covers the artwork, the headline, the chip, the description, the menu items (48px tall), the details column, and the footer buttons.

The old Overview was a different design, so this was mostly a rebuild rather than a tweak.

**What changed:**
- **Layout:** Centered hero, then description, then a two-column row with an inline action menu (Read deep dive / Watch walkthrough / View gallery) and the details (chips, role, scope).
- **Hero art:** Each project now has its own artwork:
  - **Ping:** a fanned stack of four toasts at Figma's exact positions.
  - **Undercurrent:** the logo ring. I inlined the SVG you approved downloading, so it takes the project color and nothing from the download is stored in the repo.
  - **Watchtower:** a faded CPU card (75%, +20%, stats row wrapping to "Idle 14%" like Figma) that the headline sits over.
- **Nav behavior:**
  - The Overview has no side nav and the header spans the full width, as in Figma.
  - When you move into the Deep dive, the side nav fades in and the header and footer slide to x=420 and x=430, exactly the Deep-dive frame's positions. I checked this by pressing Enter.
- **Bottom bar:** On every section it's now just Next project (X) and Back (Esc), since the Overview has its own inline menu. The footer gap is 37px on case-study pages and the nav sits 56px down, per Figma.
- **Content:** New `heroArt` field per project. Ping's Overview text and Undercurrent's scope now match Figma's copy. Undercurrent's type chip uses the pencil-ruler icon, which also applies on the Projects page.
- **Responsive and themes:** It scales down on phones (the artwork shrinks, the menu goes full width) and works in light theme.

**Please check:**
- **Fonts:** Figma's toast text is Inter, which isn't loaded on this site. I used Geist, the existing demo font, so letterforms differ slightly.
- **Toast shadows:** I kept Figma's own toast shadows, since they're part of the picture of the product UI. I read your "reuse our shadows" instruction as covering the site's UI, so say if you want that applied here too.
- **Accent red:** Figma's Ping Overview headline is a slightly more saturated red than the project color we use. I kept the project color for consistency.
- **Short windows:** I tightened the top padding on windows under 900px tall so the Overview still fits, but it will scroll slightly on very short screens.
- **Overview animation:** I rebuilt the entrance (artwork springs in, headline words rise and de-blur), but the preview pane throttles animation, so I couldn't judge its feel. Please try it in your own browser.

Should I commit this one too, then do the Deep dive frames next?
Commit the working tree changes with a sensible message.

58 59 Our hosting management app had a persistent awareness problem: users could tell that something had happened, but not always what it meant, whether it mattered, or what to do next. 60 61 I led a redesign of the notification experience to make account activity clearer, more actionable, and easier to trust. Rather than treating notifications as isolated alerts, I reframed them as part of a broader activity system and designed a dedicated inbox experience around that model. 62 63 67 68
69 70
71 72
73 74 ## The problem 75 76 The existing experience used a familiar bell-and-popover pattern, but it wasn't a good fit for the system underneath it. 77 78 Our "notifications" were actually built on top of a decade-old account activity model with inconsistent structure, vague messaging, and unpredictable content length. A single item might contain a simple server update or a few paragraphs of technical maintenance details. The UI looked modern, but the experience was hard to scan and difficult to act on. 79 80 That left users asking themselves questions like what had happened? Is this still in progress? What is it related to? Do I need to do anything? And most importantly: **Where do I go next?** 81 82
83 84
85 86 ## The solution 87 88 I redesigned the experience as a full-page destination with two connected views, an inbox for unread and relevant events and a full account history. This gave users a clearer place to check what was new, while also giving the system enough room to show meaningful detail and history. 89 90
91 92
93 94
95 96 ## The approach 97 98 A year earlier, I had tried to modernize the experience by adapting it to that more standard notification pattern. That approach didn't hold up, because the real problem wasn't visual polish, it was the underlying product model. 99 100 The system wasn't built around lightweight alerts. It was built around events and account activity. Once I stopped trying to force it into a conventional notification UI, the right direction became much clearer. Instead of designing a better popover, I designed around the structure the product already had. 101 102
103 108 113
114 115
116 117
118 119 120 The original popover constrained both the content and the mental model. Moving 121 the experience into a dedicated inbox created more room, clearer hierarchy, 122 and a stronger sense of place in the product. 123 124 125 126 127
128 129
130 131 132 The system was built around notifications containing multiple updates over 133 time, but the old interface flattened that structure. Reframing each 134 notification as a timeline of events made the interface more understandable 135 because it reflected the actual logic of the system. 136 137 138 139 140
141 142
143 144 145 The old experience surfaced information, but didn't do much to help users 146 respond. Introducing dynamic actions based on the latest event state reduced 147 the work users had to do after interpreting a message and made the system more 148 useful in the moment. 149 150 151 152 153
154 155
156 157 158 159

160 Embracing the structure of the underlying system instead of fighting it 161 was key. 162

163

164 Rather than flattening account activity into generic alerts, I used that 165 event-based model to create a clearer mental model for users, shifting the 166 experience from passive information display toward guided problem-solving. 167

168 169 170

171 This reinforced an important lesson for me: familiar UI patterns only work 172 when they match the logic of the system behind them. 173

174

175 The strongest part of this work wasn't the interface itself, it was 176 reframing the problem. Once I treated notifications as activity rather 177 than alerts, the product direction became much more coherent. 178

**Matched to Figma**
- **Layout:** the article and the side nav both start 160px down. The article column is at x=420 and the side nav at x=120.
- **Intro:** the lead paragraph is now 24px/40px (it was 28px), with 28px between blocks and a fixed 1440:882 crop on the hero screenshot.
- **Headings:** they're semibold.
- **Problem and Solution:** the Problem card sits on top with a solid fill. The Solution card tucks 24px under it, with a full-colour border and a gradient that is strongest at the bottom. Before, the Problem card lost its top padding, and the Solution gradient ran the wrong way.
- **Before/After:** this is a new component, [BeforeAfter.astro](src/components/case-study/BeforeAfter.astro). It shows two 276px-tall cropped screenshots with mono captions, and "After" takes the project colour. I only used it in Ping's approach section.
- **Numbered feature blocks:** the title is now a small project-coloured number plus a mono 20px title, with a 28px-line description under it. The numbers (01, 02, 03) count up automatically.
- **Loop videos:** they have 4px corners and a "LOOP · 5S" tag, with the length read from the video file. Ping shows 5S, 6.5S and 5S, as in Figma.
- **Postscript:** it's now three rows with a hairline divider, a small icon and mono label on the left, and the copy at x=664. The old "The postscript" heading is gone, since the Figma frame has none.
- **Side nav:** the selected item has stepped pixel corners. The sub-items have a thin vertical line with rounded elbows.

The bottom action bar now shows on load, slides down out of view as you scroll down, and slides back as soon as you scroll up. It uses the same rule as the top nav, so both bars move together. This is uncommitted on `fix/figma-case-study-deep-dive`, and lint is clean.

In the browser at 1440x1080 the bars were visible at load and hid on scroll down. They came back on scroll up, but I only saw that reliably with 1.2s waits, because the first, faster test lagged. I didn't check the slide animation itself.

- **How it works:** the existing scroll handler in [TopNav.astro](src/layouts/TopNav.astro) now toggles `data-hidden` on the bottom bar too. [BottomNav.astro](src/layouts/BottomNav.astro) has a 0.3s slide-down transition for it, turned off for reduced-motion.
- **While hidden:** the bar is inert, so its buttons can't be clicked or tabbed to. The keyboard shortcuts (X, Esc, and the rest) still work.
- **Everywhere, not just Deep dive:** the bottom bar behaves this way on every page that has one, including the Projects page, which barely scrolls.
- **Jump to a section:** jumping to a section via the side nav, Enter on the Overview, or a `#deep-dive` link counts as scrolling down. The bars hide after the jump and reappear on the first scroll up. Say if you'd rather they stay visible after those jumps.
